aliases.name: Qilin
aliases.meaning: 麒麟; the original Chinese name

description.summary: An auspicious chimerical creature of East Asian mythology — qilin in Chinese, kirin in Japanese, girin in Korean, kỳ lân in Vietnamese — said to appear at the birth or death of a sage or just ruler, and so gentle that it will not tread on living grass or eat living things.
description.full: The kirin (Japanese 麒麟; Chinese qilin; Korean girin; Vietnamese kỳ lân) is one of the most revered creatures of East Asian mythology and one of the Four Auspicious Beasts (四靈, sì líng) alongside the dragon, phoenix, and tortoise. The original Chinese qilin is a chimera — sources variously give it the body of a deer or ox, the tail of an ox, the hooves of a horse or cleft cloven hooves, scales of a fish or dragon, a dragon-like head, and one or two horns. Although Western translation often calls it the 'Chinese unicorn', the qilin is rarely depicted with a single horn; the name itself is a compound of 麒 (qí, the male) and 麟 (lín, the female). The earliest mention of the lin appears in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing, 11th–7th c. BCE), and the Spring and Autumn Annals records that Confucius identified a captured lin in 481 BCE shortly before his death — a passage central to later Confucian commentary. The kirin is gentle, will not walk on growing grass, will not eat living vegetation, and serves as an omen of the imminent birth or death of a great sage or ruler. In Japanese culture the kirin retains all this lore but is also the modern Japanese word for the giraffe — a usage that dates to the Ming dynasty, when the giraffes brought back from Africa by the eunuch admiral Zheng He's voyages (early 15th century) were celebrated at the Chinese court as living qilin. The figure is heavily represented in East Asian visual culture (komainu-style stone guardians, palace iconography, and the heraldry of Buddhist temples) and remains a major motif in modern manga, anime, and video games.

etymology.origin: Chinese 麒麟 (qílín), in which 麒 (qí) names the male and 麟 (lín) the female. Borrowed into Japanese as 'kirin', Korean as 'girin/kirin', and Vietnamese as 'kỳ lân'.
etymology.meaning: An auspicious chimerical beast; literally a male/female pair-word, treated as a single species name.
etymology.first_use: Earliest known reference is in the poem 'Lin zhi zhi' (麟之趾, 'Feet of the Lin') in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing), 11th–7th century BCE.

taxonomy.subtype: One of the Four Auspicious Beasts
taxonomy.variant: Chinese qilin / Japanese kirin / Korean girin / Vietnamese kỳ lân

coloration: multicoloured (five colours associated with the cardinal directions)

features.description: A composite of deer or ox body, ox tail, dragon head, scales, and cloven or horse-like hooves
Typically depicted with two horns or antlers in Chinese tradition; depictions vary across cultures and eras
Dragon-like scales over the body in many depictions
Often shown with flame-like adornments along the back or surrounding the body
Some Chinese and Japanese depictions add a dragon-like beard

physical.morphology: A chimera — never a simple unicorn-like horse — combining attributes of dragon, deer, ox, and fish across regional variants.

abilities.description: Appears at the birth or death of a sage, just ruler, or moment of great virtue
So gentle it does not tread on living grass or eat living plants; will not harm any being
In some traditions can recognize and punish the unrighteous, particularly corrupt judges (a role echoed in the related haetae)
Buddhist and folk-Daoist motifs depict the kirin carrying sages or holy texts

behavior.diet: Vegetarian; will not eat living plants
patterns: Manifests rarely, only in periods of great virtue or great change
Strongly associated with imperial legitimacy and the rule of the Way (dao)

range.description: Throughout the East Asian cultural sphere — China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam — and in adjacent traditions of Mongolia, Tibet, and Thailand.

first_recorded.source: Classic of Poetry (Shijing), poem 'Lin zhi zhi'

peak_activity_periods.period: Han to Tang dynasties (3rd c. BCE – 10th c. CE)
peak_activity_periods.description: Establishment of the qilin within Confucian and Daoist ritual culture
Identification of the giraffe as a living qilin during Zheng He's voyages, fixing the giraffe-kirin double meaning that persists in Japanese and Korean today

origins.cultural_roots: Ancient Chinese cosmological thought; the qilin emerges as a member of the Four Auspicious Beasts in early Confucian and Han-dynasty cosmography. Identified with the eastern direction in Han five-element schemata in some texts.
origins.earliest_accounts: Earliest written reference in the Classic of Poetry (11th–7th c. BCE); celebrated story of Confucius and the captured lin in the Spring and Autumn Annals (481 BCE).
origins.folklore_connections: Travels with Buddhism and Confucianism into Korea and Japan in the early medieval period; in Japan kirin become guardian figures and the modern word for giraffe.

timeline.event: Earliest reference to the lin in the poem 'Lin zhi zhi' in the Classic of Poetry
According to the Spring and Autumn Annals, a unicorn-like beast (lin) is captured during a hunt; Confucius identifies it as a lin and weeps, taking it as an omen of the Zhou dynasty's decline
timeline.significance: Anchors the qilin in classical Confucian narrative

timeline.event: A giraffe brought from East Africa by the eunuch admiral Zheng He's fleet is presented to the Yongle Emperor at the Ming court and celebrated as a living qilin
timeline.significance: Fixes the giraffe-as-kirin double meaning in East Asian languages
timeline.source: Ming Shilu and Ming-court paintings (e.g., Shen Du's 1414 'Tribute Giraffe')

timeline.event: Toriyama Sekien depicts the kirin in his Japanese yōkai-adjacent compendium imagery, contributing to the modern Japanese visual canon

history.modern_era: The kirin remains ubiquitous in East Asian heraldry, calligraphy, and design (e.g., the Kirin Brewery logo, Japan, 1888), and is a recurring stock figure in manga, anime, JRPGs, and martial-arts cinema. In modern Japanese and Korean it is also the everyday word for the giraffe.

documentary.name: Classic of Poetry — 'Lin zhi zhi'
documentary.description: Earliest known mention of the lin (the qilin's female form), used as an emblem of the virtuous nobility.

documentary.name: Spring and Autumn Annals — capture of the lin
documentary.description: Confucius identifies a captured beast as a lin and reads it as an omen.

documentary.name: Shen Du — 'Tribute Giraffe with Attendant'
documentary.description: Ming court painting depicting the East African giraffe brought back by Zheng He's fleet, celebrated as a qilin.
documentary.source: Philadelphia Museum of Art (extant copies); discussed by Sally K. Church and others

paranormal.name: Genuine auspicious manifestation
paranormal.description: In classical Confucian, Daoist, and East Asian Buddhist thought, the kirin is a genuine spiritual being whose appearance is an objective sign from heaven.

scientific.name: Giraffe identification (Ming dynasty and after)
scientific.description: The Ming court's celebration of giraffes as living qilin reflects a real-world identification driven by the giraffe's exotic morphology — long neck, mottled coat, gentle disposition — and is the origin of the modern Japanese / Korean usage of kirin / girin for the giraffe.
evidence_cited: Continued use of 麒麟 / 기린 / kỳ lân for 'giraffe' in modern East Asian languages

scientific.name: Sivatherium / extinct giraffid hypothesis
scientific.description: A minority popular hypothesis suggests that the qilin's chimerical features may preserve cultural memory of extinct giraffids such as Sivatherium; this is speculative and not mainstream paleontological consensus.
evidence_cited: Morphological features (cleft hooves, ox-like body, ossicone-like horns) shared with extinct giraffids

skeptical.name: Mythical composite, not a real species
skeptical.description: Mainstream scholarship treats the qilin/kirin as a culturally constructed chimera assembled from familiar animal parts to symbolize virtue, harmony, and imperial legitimacy.
evidence_cited: Stable composite iconography from the Han dynasty onward
Use in imperial heraldry and ritual rather than zoological catalogues

traditions: Confucian narrative tradition surrounding Confucius and the captured lin
Imperial Chinese, Korean, Japanese, and Vietnamese court iconography
stories: Confucius's reaction to the captured lin (481 BCE)
The Ming court's reception of Zheng He's giraffe as a qilin (1414)
Folktales of kirin appearing at the births of Confucius and other sages
folklore.beliefs: Sign of heaven's approval; embodiment of virtue, gentleness, and just rulership.

literature: Hayashi Razan and other Edo-period scholars on the kirin
Modern Japanese fantasy literature (e.g., the Twelve Kingdoms by Fuyumi Ono)

Various Japanese anime and Korean historical dramas
